title: Resolving Disputes
subtitle: The Buddha's Framework for Harmony in Community
epigraph: You do not understand this Dharma and discipline. I understand this Dharma and discipline.

segments.text: This evening we're looking at the Samagama Sutta discourse. And this is concerning the Jains again, so this is what happened according to the Buddhist propaganda, you might say. I don't know whether this happened or not, but definitely something happened when the Nagantha, the leader of the Jains, died.
And this is what is said. On his death, the Naganthas divided, split into two, and they had taken to quarreling and brawling and were deep in dispute, stabbing each other with verbal daggers.

"You do not understand this Dharma and discipline. I understand this Dharma and discipline. How could you understand this Dharma and discipline? Your way is wrong. My way is right. I am consistent. You are inconsistent. What should have been said first, you said last. What should have been said last, you said first. What you had so carefully thought up has been turned inside out. Your assertion has been shown up. You are refuted. Go and learn better or disentangle yourself if you can."

Daggers definitely. So it seems there was nothing but slaughter amongst the Negantha's pupils. I think that's a bit of an older statement. I don't think you mean it physically. And the white clothed lay disciples were disgusted, dismayed and disappointed with the Negantha's pupils as they were with so badly proclaimed and badly expounded dharma and discipline, which was un-emancipating, unconducive to peace, expounded by one not fully enlightened, and was now with its shrine broken, left without a refuge. So that's a bit of Buddhist propaganda, I think.

Anyway, the novice Chunda, who was seemingly a younger brother of Sariputta, was spending the rains where the Nigantha supposedly died in Parva. And he met Ananda and he told Ananda about all these goings on. And Ananda said, well, we'd better go and have a chat with the Buddha, with the Blessed One. So they tell the Blessed One, the Buddha, everything that's been happening.

And the Buddha replies, "What do you think, Ananda? These things that I have taught you directly, in other words, my teachings—that is, the 37 factors that lead to liberation, the Bodhi Pakiya Dhamma, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right kinds of striving, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the Noble Eightfold Path. I'm sure you understand all those. Do you see even two bhikkhus who make differing assertions about these things? Do you see any disputes arising?"

"No, Venerable Sir, I do not even see two monks or monastics differing about this. But Venerable Sir, there are people who live deferential towards the Blessed One who might, when he's gone, create a dispute in the Sangha about livelihood and about patimokha, the rule. Now, such a dispute would be for the harm and unhappiness of many, for the loss, harm and suffering of gods and humans."

The Buddha replies, a dispute about livelihood or about patimokha—livelihood, how they live. Remember the bhikkhus stands for all, for the four assemblies: monks, nuns, laywomen, laymen. So dispute about livelihood or about the patimokha. The patimokha here is, of course, the specific rules, the institutional rules that govern the order. But as lay people, you can take it as the moral law.

He said a dispute about that would be trifling. But should a dispute arise in the sangha about the path and the way, such a dispute would be for the harm and unhappiness of many, the loss, harm and suffering of gods and men. So he was much more concerned about the Dharma.

Now he says there are six roots to disputes, and I think most of these we will recognize. You can bring this into your daily life where you've seen it in the place of work, amongst your friends, and so on, and of course in politics.

So someone is angry and revengeful and dwells disrespectful and undeferential towards the teacher, towards the Dharma, towards the Sangha, does not fulfill the training. Now, if we see any such root of dispute, either in ourselves or externally, you should strive to abandon the same evil root of dispute and make sure that it does not arise in the future. So that's the great effort. That's one of the great efforts, isn't it, to let go of something that's unwholesome and to stop the unwholesomeness arising. So the first one is this business of anger and revenge.
Then there's contempt. So that anger and revenge could be, for instance, of an employee towards the employer. Contemptuous and domineering could be the employer towards the employee.
Then, of course, there's always envy and avarice, wanting what other people have.
There's deceit and fraud, fiddling.
There's evil wishes and wrong view. That's basically wishing somebody that they drop dead or something.
And there are those who adhere to their own views tenaciously and relinquish them with difficulty, even when they're wrong. They won't negotiate, they won't compromise.

Then he says there are four kinds of litigation. So this is where things have to be sorted out. Litigation because of dispute, litigation because of accusation, because of an offence, and concerning proceedings. So there are four reasons why you take things to court in the order anyway. The first one is to try and work out the dispute, the disagreement. The second one is to sort out an accusation that's been made against somebody. Then there's one concerning a specific offence. And there's one about proceedings.
And in order to sort this out, there are seven kinds of settlements. So then it becomes clear what these four things are. And again, this has a direct connection with ordinary daily life.

The removal by confrontation. So there's a dispute, much like the Jains. "It is the Dharma. It is not the Dharma. This is the discipline. This is not the discipline," et cetera, et cetera. Now, what the Buddha says is that everybody should meet in concord. In other words, to come with a heart of goodwill. And having met together, the guideline of the Dharma should be drawn out. In other words, they should actually discuss the way, the teaching. So he's preparing the order for when he's not there, remember. And once the guideline has been drawn out, the litigation should be settled in a way which accords with it.

Now, supposing that doesn't work, there is the opinion of the majority. If those bhikkhus cannot settle that litigation in that dwelling place, they should go to a dwelling place where there's a greater number of bhikkhus. So in other words, you go to a different court, a higher court for some guidance and for the decision. So the opinion of the majority settles the dispute.
Now the next three are to do with individual offences. So this is more like people who commit crimes.

So the first one is a litigation on account of memory. So here a monk reproves another monk. This is more to do with monks, but as I say, you can easily transfer it into ordinary daily life. So somebody reproves somebody else of such a grave offence. In this case, it's one involving defeat or bordering on defeat. Remember, the rules of defeat are killing, stealing, any sexual intercourse, and creating a split in the Sangha, in the order of monks. So it would be creating hate speech in society, things like that.
So now the question is, "Does the Venerable One remember having committed such a grave offence involving defeat?"
"I do not, friends. I do not remember having committed such and such a grave offence."

In this case, the removal of litigation on account of memory should be pronounced. So in other words, this looks as though the witnesses, or there were no witnesses, it may just have been hearsay, and we have to give the benefit of the doubt to the Bhikkhu here who says that he doesn't remember that at all, that somebody's defaming him.
Now, the next one is by litigation on account of past insanity. So here a Bhikkhu reproves another Bhikkhu of such a grave offense involving this defeat.
"Does the Venerable One remember having committed such a grave offense involving defeat?"
"I do not remember having done so."
Despite the denial, the former presses the latter further. "Surely the Venerable One must know quite well if he remembers having committed such and such an offense."
And he says, "Oh, I had gone mad, friend. I was out of my mind. And when I was mad, I said and did many things improper for a recluse, but I do not remember. I was mad when I did it."
So in this case, because he's mad, the litigation is removed. It's not taken any further.

He might of course be lying, but some of you might have read a book called The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat, which was quite a bestseller—oh, I don't know, 80s or something. It was written by a man called Oliver Sacks who is a great psychiatrist, writer about mental diseases. And there was a case in there of a man who murdered and really did a lot of damage to his daughter. And if I remember rightly, it was an adopted daughter. And he couldn't remember, and he was believed that he couldn't remember, and he was put into a mental home.

And while he was in the mental home, the nurses and people around him became more and more confident about him, and they would allow him out on a bicycle ride. So one day while he's riding a bicycle, he hits something and he bumps his head and he remembers what he did. And according to Oliver Sacks, it took them six months to stop him from trying to commit suicide. So things can happen where you just basically forget. Anyway, that's called madness. And as we've seen it, it probably is.

Now there's another one which is the effecting acknowledgement of an offense. So in this case, a monk has done something wrong. He accepts it and he goes and apologizes. He reveals it and he discloses it. He goes to a senior bhikkhu and after arranging his robe, paying homage at his feet and then sitting to the side, palms together saying, "Venerable sir, I've committed such and such an offense and I confess it."
And the response is, "Do you see what you've done?"
He says, "Yes, I do."
"Will you practice restraint in the future?"
"I will practice restraint in the future."

Now this is only for the lesser rules. And every half moon, the monks get together to do this confession. And this is the actual dialogue, where you say you've committed so many offences—you don't have to actually name them, although in some orders you do. And the response is, "Do you see what you've done?" You say, "I have, I've seen what I've done." "Will you restrain in the future?" "I will restrain." Every two weeks, as it were, the slate is wiped clean. But remember, this is only for the lesser offences.

Then there's the pronouncement of bad character against someone. So here, somebody is reproved of a great offence, one involving defeat, et cetera. And again, he says, "I do not remember having committed the grave offence." Despite the denial, the former presses. Again, he denies it. And again, despite the denial, the former presses again. And finally, he does actually admit it.

So this reminds you of sort of libel cases, really, where somebody is trying to defend themselves against libel. And eventually, of course, the libel wasn't libel at all, but it was true. And, of course, such a person, they have a pronouncement of bad character against someone.

So if the order does that, I'm not exactly sure as to what that means, but probably he says, "I remember having committed such a grave offense, one involving defeat or bordering on defeat. I was hurried. I was confused. When I said that I did not remember having committed such and such a grave offense, one involving such a thing." Such a pronouncement of bad character against someone. And so there comes a settlement on this.

And I think once somebody has bad character, he has to leave that monastery probably. And once he's done that, he's got to find some other support from somewhere. If the lay people begin to recognise that he's not behaving properly as a monastic, they can refuse to offer him food, et cetera. Eventually, he could be driven just to disrobe.
And the final one, I think, is a lovely way to deal with something. It's called covering over with grass. It's not the same as sweeping under the carpet, right, trying to forget it.

So here there's quarreling and brawling, deep disputes, that they may have said and done many improper things. And so they should all meet together, and they try to come to some sort of agreement about things. But the disputes and the brawling are far too much. And for the good of these, benevolence for their own, I shall confess. So there's an inability for them to come to some sort of an agreement. And so the thing is to put grass over it and let it simmer for a while. Let it just rest for a while. When the heat's gone out of the argument, then it's possible to bring it back.

And then finally, he says these six memorable qualities that create love and respect and conduce to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to concord and to unity. Now, this is repeated in another discourse that we'll be doing tomorrow. And we'll be looking at the actual dispute that arises, which gives us some idea as to what monks can get up to.

So I hope that at least it's been informative and has increased your confidence in the Buddha and his teachings and that this will drive you on to liberate yourself from all suffering sooner rather than later.
